newsitem.title: USA: U.S. home sales seen healthy, but data volatile.
newsitem.headline: U.S. home sales seen healthy, but data volatile.

text.p: Robust home sales data in June indicated a healthy U.S. housing market but a sharp downward revision in May sales numbers pointed to the volatile nature of housing data, U.S. economists said Wednesday.
Earlier, the Commerce Department reported June single -family home sales rose 6.1 percent, but revised May data showed a one percent rise instead of a 7.1 percent jump.
The U.S. Treasury market built on recent gains after the data's release.

Dan Seto, economist at Nikko Securities, said the Commerce Department basically shifted a lot of the recovery from May to June. The data for June showed a seasonally adjusted annual rate of 819,000. May's annual rate, previously reported at 825,000, was revised to 772,000.

"These numbers really illustrate that the fundamentals are strong and are paving the way for new activity in housing," said Anthony Chan, Banc One Investment Advisors chief economist. Chan added that the firm tone in June data suggested the housing market would be a positive contributing factor to the U.S. economy in the third quarter.
Analysts cautioned that substantial revisions to May data illustrated the volatile nature of the data.
"I think the housing market likely will stay strong with the rate of home sales over 800,000," said Lynn Reaser, chief economist at Barnett Banks Inc.
Reaser pointed out that in 1996, the level of annual home sales was 757,000. In the nine years prior to 1996, she added, the annual sales level ranged between 500,000 and 700,000.
But, Reaser cautioned, "there appears to be a lot of volatility."

The Barnett Bank chief economist said that the June level of 819,000 appeared more realistic and more in line with economic conditions in the second quarter. Reaser added that if sales held at a level higher than 800,000, the potential for further upside was limited.
The June number reflected lower borrowing costs and a more upbeat consumer, economists said.

"Tight labor markets and consumer confidence overall are higher and mortgage rates are declining," said Chan. He predicted that as long as supply of homes for sale remained below six months, the housing sector would continue to expand.
As reported, the supply of homes for sale declined to 4.2 months's worth in June, its lowest reading since 4.1 months' worth in July 1971.
The benchmark 30-year Treasury bond was up 15/32 as the report was released, but rallied 29/32 higher to yield 6.32 percent just after 1100 EDT/1500 GMT.
The effect of these numbers on Treasuries was negligible, said Kevin Flanagan, economist at Dean Witter Reynolds Inc.
